title: Museum of Bottled Water
text:
The Museum of Bottled Water was founded on the idea that bottled water is one of the objects that define our age. To understand bottled water as an object is to see industrial production, globalization, and marketing instantiated in an anodyne commodity. According to Reuters, in 2018 almost one million plastic water bottles were purchased every minute, 1.3 billion plastic bottles purchased every day. The process for blowing polyethylene terephthalate pellets into bottles was first developed in 1973 by Nathaniel Wyeth, brother of the artist Andrew Wyeth.
Containerized shipping: Perrier -important as a model of production globalization The story of Perrier’s creation of the bottled water industry deserves its own essay.
That should remind us that the bottled water industry is actually quite old. If we are willing to slightly shift our focus from bottled water to packaged water a slightly different understanding opens up. In the current moment cartons, cans, bags, etc. If we look to the past the story of human development can be told through the technologies used
In our contemporary moment of rapine with the planet that sustains us, some people come to the museum of bottled water wanting to know
Blair Schulman wrote an article about the last public installation of the museum for Hyperallergic.
 The Museum of Bottled Water was a collaborative effort. Tim Harte created the soundtrack for the museum. Elvis Achelpohl was the chief architect. Seth Johnson did the graphic design. Hadley Clark made the docent’s uniform. EG Schempf documented the installations. Charlie Miley illustrated some of the collection. Lacey Wozny assisted with project management. Adam Crowley assisted with preparations work. Elliot Oliver consulted about insurance. I tried to celebrate the collaborative reality of the project by hanging a banner with the museum’s logo surrounded by the logos of the team. Amy Frogpockets emborydered the banner.  The Museum is currently on hiatus and our collection in long-term storage as we contemplate the next iteration of the project.
That said, new items are occasionally added to the collection.

title: a pairing
text:
I grew up playing music every day, writing songs and constantly thinking about my bands. Some day I’ll upload music from my high school reggae band, my glam rock band from College, and the bedroom rock album I made in my 20’s. Something, someting hot on 78. When I play music now it is generally with Shawn Hansen. ​
Shawn and I first played music together in the pop group Monogram in a fit of pre-9/11 optimism. Monogram started off playing songs about the seven wonders of the world with a seven wonders theme added in to make eight songs. The band was hot, but few recordings were made. One by one the group peeled off, took a sabbatical, started a new band or left town.
Eventually, Shawn and I playing got together again on Kansas City’s Westside while we all white-knuckled through the hangover from the Great Financial Crisis. Maybe because we were thinking a lot about food at the time, maybe because there were only two of us, we decided to call ourselves a pairing instead of a duo and the name has stuck. Over the past decade or so Shawn has a released half-dozen or so recordings of our playing. He does most of the work cleaning up our sessions, selecting the parts, packaging and sharing them online. All the while Shawn has been prolifically collaborating and releasing his own music, I highly recommend his albums Frenzy, Radio Badlands, and Want Cry Love to get a sense of his range.




Curling When The Crisis Hits (2026) A Pairing



​​I described this, our most recent release, to a friend as improvised microtonal music, though that may not be strictly speaking accurate. I’m playing a nice instrument here, borrowed from Johnny Hammill with one of his French bows alternating with a short bow made by Tatsuya Nakatani for bowing cymbals. I generally don’t like the timbre of the bass when I bow it, nevertheless, I make a point of playing with a bow when I get the chance—hoping that through repetition I will improve. Listening back to these recordings I hear the an anxiety in my sound that is familiar and appropriate for these songs.
